Understanding doubly robust methods

Source: vignettes/doubly-robust.Rmd
doubly-robust.Rmd

How can we estimate a treatment effect when treated and untreated patients differ at baseline? This introduction compares inverse probability weighting, outcome-model standardization, and doubly robust estimation. It then shows how to use precmed for a binary outcome. For the formulas and outcome-specific assumptions, see Methods for estimating average treatment effects.

The question and the models

Suppose the outcome is whether a patient has a relapse during one year. We want the population-average risk difference: the proportion who would relapse if everyone received treatment 1 minus the proportion who would relapse if everyone received treatment 0. A negative difference means fewer relapses under treatment 1. This marginal effect is distinct from a treatment effect conditional on a particular patient’s covariates.

In observational data, the observed difference in relapse proportions may reflect differences in baseline characteristics as well as treatment. Two approaches can help adjust for measured covariates:

  • Inverse probability weighting (IPW) uses a treatment model to estimate each patient’s propensity score: the probability of receiving treatment 1 given their covariates. Patients receive more weight if they received a treatment that was less likely given their covariates. The weighted relapse outcomes are then compared between treatment groups. Propensity scores can also be used for matching, stratification, or regression adjustment; see Chapter 7 for an introduction to these methods (Jiang et al. 2026).
  • Outcome-model standardization, also called g-computation, uses an outcome model to predict relapse given treatment and covariates. For each patient in the target population, the model predicts the probability of relapse under treatment 0 and again under treatment 1, using the patient’s observed covariates. Averaging the predictions separately for each treatment gives two estimated population-average risks; their difference estimates the risk difference. For example, average predicted risks of 20% under treatment 0 and 15% under treatment 1 give a risk difference of -5 percentage points.

Both approaches need causal identification assumptions, including well-defined treatments and consistency, no unmeasured treatment–outcome confounding given the adjustment covariates, and positivity: each treatment must be possible at relevant covariate values. They also need suitable modeling and regularity assumptions. Outcome-model standardization generally relies on a correctly specified outcome model, whereas IPW relies on a correctly specified treatment model. These are sometimes called singly robust approaches with respect to model misspecification. Rather than calling them “non-robust,” it is more informative to say which assumptions each approach requires.

What does doubly robust mean?

A doubly robust estimator combines the outcome and treatment models in a particular way. For example, augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) starts with outcome-model predictions and adds a propensity-weighted correction based on the observed prediction errors. Under the identification and relevant regularity assumptions, this estimator is consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is correctly specified; both may be correct (Kurz 2022). Merely fitting two models does not make an estimator doubly robust.

Outcome model Treatment model AIPW consistency under the other assumptions
Correct Correct Yes
Correct Incorrect Yes
Incorrect Correct Yes
Incorrect Incorrect Not guaranteed

This is an asymptotic property, not a promise of negligible bias in a finite sample or valid confidence intervals without further conditions. Double robustness does not fix unmeasured confounding, poor overlap, measurement errors, or misspecification of both models. Extreme propensity scores can make estimates unstable. Truncating propensity scores may improve stability, but if it changes the true probabilities it can remove the guarantee based solely on a correct treatment model. Examine overlap and model plausibility rather than treating double robustness as a substitute for study design.

An example with a binary outcome

The following synthetic example compares three estimates of the same population-average risk difference, treatment 1 minus treatment 0, for relapse within one year. Treatment assignment depends on age and previous treatment. The outcome is fully observed. The simulation is illustrative, not a clinical estimate; its treatment model is correctly specified by construction, while the generated outcome need not follow the logistic outcome model exactly. A single simulated dataset cannot establish which estimator is unbiased.

library(precmed)
dat <- simulate_binary(n = 4000, seed = 2026, followup = 1, threshold = 0)
table(dat$trt)
#> 
#> drug0 drug1 
#>  1858  2142

First, fit a logistic outcome model and average predictions for the same patients under each treatment. Then fit a logistic treatment model and calculate IPW means. These are illustrative base R calculations, not separate precmed estimators. We include treatment interactions in the outcome model and use the same covariates in both approaches below.

outcome_fit <- glm(y ~ trt * (age + previous_treatment),
                   data = dat, family = binomial())
treatment_fit <- glm(trt ~ age + previous_treatment,
                     data = dat, family = binomial())

under_0 <- under_1 <- dat
under_0$trt <- factor("drug0", levels = levels(dat$trt))
under_1$trt <- factor("drug1", levels = levels(dat$trt))
standardized <- mean(predict(outcome_fit, under_1, type = "response")) -
  mean(predict(outcome_fit, under_0, type = "response"))

# Match the default propensity-score limits used by atefit().
ps <- pmin(pmax(predict(treatment_fit, type = "response"), 0.01), 0.99)
treated <- dat$trt == "drug1"
ipw <- mean(treated * dat$y / ps) - mean((!treated) * dat$y / (1 - ps))

Now fit the doubly robust AIPW estimator with atefit(). cate.model specifies the outcome and covariates; atefit() adds treatment and, by default, treatment–covariate interactions. ps.model specifies the treatment model. The 50 bootstrap replicates keep this example quick; use more for a substantive analysis and examine bootstrap diagnostics.

fit <- atefit(response = "binary", data = dat,
              cate.model = y ~ age + previous_treatment,
              ps.model = trt ~ age + previous_treatment,
              n.boot = 50, seed = 999)
c(outcome_standardization = standardized, ipw = ipw,
  doubly_robust = unname(fit$risk.difference$estimate))
#> outcome_standardization                     ipw           doubly_robust 
#>             -0.10298071             -0.09978176             -0.10762720
confint(fit)
#>                      2.5 %      97.5 %
#> risk.difference -0.1421899 -0.07306452

The estimates need not agree in a finite sample, even when the necessary assumptions hold. The displayed confidence interval applies to the atefit() estimate, not the two illustrative calculations. A confidence interval describes sampling uncertainty under the procedure; it does not account for unmeasured confounding or establish that either model is correct.

Choosing and using a method

Doubly robust estimation can be useful when there is uncertainty about the correct specification of the outcome and treatment models. A singly robust approach, such as outcome-model standardization or inverse probability weighting, generally relies on correct specification of its respective model. A doubly robust estimator such as AIPW is consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is correctly specified, provided the required causal identification and regularity assumptions also hold. Note that doubly robust methods do not protect against unmeasured confounding, poor treatment overlap, or misspecification of both models.

Doubly robust estimation is not automatically more accurate in every dataset. Specify both models carefully using subject-matter knowledge, inspect treatment overlap and extreme weights, assess model fit and sensitivity to modeling choices, and report the target population and effect scale. Randomization can support exchangeability, but overlap and other assumptions still matter. For a simple randomized trial, an intercept-only treatment model may be appropriate; account for the actual assignment design when choosing it.

In precmed, atefit() estimates a marginal risk difference for binary outcomes, a marginal rate ratio for count outcomes, and, for survival outcomes at a chosen horizon, a marginal restricted mean time lost ratio, cumulative hazard ratio, and event risk difference (treatment 1 minus treatment 0). The catefit() methods instead construct covariate-conditional treatment-effect scores; some scoring methods are doubly robust, while others use different approaches. Score fitting and subsequent validation are distinct tasks, and an ATE estimate or its bootstrap interval is not validation of a CATE score. See Methods for developing and validating CATE scores for method-specific details and assumptions.

For survival outcomes, precmed also uses a censoring model to supply probabilities for inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW). Double robustness with respect to the outcome and treatment models does not protect against a misspecified censoring model. The estimand and support at the chosen survival horizon matter too. For example, an out-of-range restricted mean survival estimate may trigger an outcome-model fallback that does not retain the doubly robust guarantee. See Methods for estimating average treatment effects for these qualifications and the survival estimands.
